title: From Model to Classroom: Evaluating Generated MCQs for Portuguese with Narrative and Difficulty Concerns
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI models can produce reading-comprehension multiple-choice questions (MCQs) suitable for Portuguese elementary classrooms, and how those generated items compare with human-authored questions. The authors focus on two practical challenges in educational question generation: controlling narrative alignment (e.g., character, feeling, action, causal relationship) and controlling difficulty levels for young readers. They also explicitly investigate failure cases, because the paper is motivated by concerns that generated items may be unreliable in real classroom use.

The study compares three generation pipelines: GPT-4o in a one-step prompting setup, Gemma-2 in a one-step prompting setup, and a two-step pipeline using a fine-tuned ptt5-v2 model to generate the wh-question followed by Gemma-2 to generate options and difficulty. The content consists of 12 narrative texts recommended for Portuguese elementary education, and the resulting MCQs were evaluated by 18 Portuguese-language experts in education/learning-resource development. The authors then filtered validated items and administered 124 MCQs to 284 students across 14 classes in Portuguese schools to estimate psychometric properties such as difficulty and discrimination.

Overall, the paper concludes that GPT-4o and Gemma-2 generated MCQs of broadly comparable quality to human-authored items in terms of expert acceptance, psychometric difficulty, and discrimination, although human items still had slight advantages in distractor quality and some psychometric measures. The two-step pipeline performed worse, especially on answerability and distractor reliability. Reported limitations and risks include semantic ambiguity, unclear option wording, answerability failures, use of the wrong Portuguese variant (Brazilian instead of European Portuguese), and distractors that are less engaging or less plausible than human-authored ones. The authors argue that generative AI can be useful for MCQ creation, but classroom use requires careful validation and still does not fully match human item construction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based generative AI chatbot/model family used for text generation and instruction-following tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a one-step zero-shot prompting setup to generate Portuguese reading-comprehension MCQs with question, correct answer, distractors, difficulty, and narrative label.

findings.finding_summary: Expert review found GPT-4o-generated MCQs were largely acceptable and comparable to human-authored items. Well-formed wh-questions were 40/45 (88.9%), option clarity was 38/42 (90.5%), answerability was 33/38 (86.8%), and narrative alignment was 42/42 (100%); experts noted some semantic issues and unclear options, but overall quality was close to human-authored MCQs.
findings.measure: Expert ratings of well-formedness, narrative alignment, options clarity, and answerability

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s Gemini family of generative AI models used for text generation and instruction-following tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a one-step zero-shot prompting setup to generate Portuguese reading-comprehension MCQs; the paper refers to Gemma-2-27B as Gemma-2.

findings.finding_summary: Expert review found Gemma-2-generated MCQs were broadly comparable to human-authored MCQs, though with more issues than GPT-4o in several dimensions. Well-formed wh-questions were 33/45 (73.3%), option clarity was 35/41 (85.4%), answerability was 33/35 (94.3%), and narrative alignment was 41/41 (100%); experts reported semantic problems and unclear options, but no statistically significant differences were found in distractor plausibility or difficulty versus other provenances.
findings.measure: Expert ratings of well-formedness, narrative alignment, options clarity, answerability, distractor plausibility, and difficulty

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s Gemini family of generative AI models used for text generation and instruction-following tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a two-step pipeline with ptt5-v2-large to generate the remaining MCQ components after the wh-question was produced.

findings.finding_summary: The two-step ptt5-v2+Gemma-2 approach performed worse on several expert-review measures than the one-step LLM approaches. Well-formed wh-questions were 38/45 (84.4%), option clarity was 37/39 (94.9%), but answerability was only 25/37 (67.6%), and experts noted multiple valid answers, mismatches, and ambiguity; the paper concludes the two-step method may not be effective for MCQ creation.
findings.measure: Expert ratings of well-formedness, options clarity, and answerability

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model systems used for automated text and question generation without a single named product being studied.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies current generative models for producing Portuguese reading-comprehension MCQs and compares them to human-authored items and a fine-tuned encoder-decoder baseline.

findings.finding_summary: Across the study, generated MCQs were often comparable to human-authored ones, but limitations and risks were identified. Reported issues included semantic ambiguity, unclear or nonsensical questions, distractors that were less plausible than human-authored ones, answerability failures, and a recurring tendency to output Brazilian Portuguese instead of the requested European Portuguese; the two-step generation setup performed especially poorly on answerability and reliability.
findings.measure: Expert review and psychometric analysis of generated MCQs versus human-authored MCQs
findings.sample_size: n=238 MCQs for expert review; n=124 validated MCQs for student psychometrics

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study with expert review and student-response psychometrics, but it is not a controlled intervention trial. The evidence is useful and detailed, yet it is observational/measurement-based rather than causal.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports mostly descriptive comparisons and no effect sizes for learning outcomes, so the classroom impact is unclear. It does identify practical risks and quality limitations, but not medium or large instructional gains.
